user_input: How many GPUs in Jupyter Notebook / Jupyterlab can reach the same calculation ability as A100?
response:
The number of GPUs required in a Jupyter Notebook or Jupyterlab to reach the calculation ability of an NVIDIA A100 depends on the specific GPU model being used. Different GPU models have varying compute capabilities, memory capacities, and architectural features. Factors such as the nature of the computations (e.g., data size, type of operations), memory requirements, software optimizations, and the efficiency of GPU utilization will also influence this.

Therefore, without specifics on the GPU model being used in the Jupyter Notebook/Jupyterlab and the exact computational task, I can't provide a precise number. However, given that the A100 is one of the most powerful and advanced GPUs currently available from NVIDIA, it is likely that multiple GPUs of a lesser model would be needed to match its computational capability.

For accurate estimations, I would recommend using NVIDIA's GPU comparison resources or reaching out to NVIDIA directly with details of the exact computation and GPU model.

Remember that utilizing multiple GPUs effectively could require knowledge of parallel computing. It may also introduce additional complications, such as ensuring efficient data communication between GPUs and managing potential GPU memory limitations.

user_input: How much does it cost to run jobs?
response: The FASRC (Faculty of Arts and Sciences Research Computing) system doesn't charge users for running jobs. It operates on a fairshare policy - the more you use it, the lower your priority becomes in the queue system. This ensures that all users have fair access to the resources. However, over-requesting resources can negatively affect your fairshare score, so it's important to accurately request resources for your jobs.

user_input: My job is getting stuck (currently on partition huce_bigmem) and writing to scratch.
response:
The job might be getting stuck due to insufficient memory allocation. Ensure that you've correctly allocated the necessary resources for your job, especially the memory. Remember, in Slurm, the allocated memory is strict - you must ensure that you request enough memory for your task using the --mem option.
In the provided context, the huce_bigmem partition is designed for large memory work, requiring greater than 1000 GB RAM per job. If your job requests less than 1000 GB RAM, it will be automatically rejected by the scheduler.
If you don't specify the amount of memory your task requires, the system defaults to 100 MB which might not be enough for your job, causing it to get stuck.
Finally, always check that your inputs, outputs, and error specifications are correct in your Slurm script to prevent errors. You might want to test your job first using the --test-only option in Slurm to see if there are any issues before submitting the job fully.
If you've checked all these factors and still face the issue, it might be due to something specific in your job or it could be a potential system error.

I keep getting into problems on Odyssey/Cannon because, when I create new files, they tend to be assigned to the group "super_lab" and not "incredible_lab". The former has very little disk space available, while the latter has a lot.

This becomes a real problem when I try to untar a large tar_file. The output files are assigned to the group "narayan_lab" and there is not enough disk space. What should I do?
response:
It sounds like you might have to change your default group. In a Unix-based system, each user can belong to one or more groups. When you create a file, by default it will be assigned to your primary group, which in your case might be "super_lab".
Here is how you can change your default group to "incredible_lab":
Check your current groups with the groups command. This will give you a list of groups you are a member of, with your default group first.

If "incredible_lab" is listed, you can change your default group to it using the newgrp command followed by the group name, like this: newgrp incredible_lab.

This will start a new shell session with "incredible_lab" as your default group. Any files that you create in this session will be assigned to the "incredible_lab" group.
Remember this change is only for this session. If you log out and back in, your default group will reset to "super_lab". If "incredible_lab" should always be your default group, you might have to contact your system administrator to help you make that change.
Please try to untar the file after changing your default group, and let me know if you still encounter issues.

user_input: Would it be possible to install VirtualGL (https://virtualgl.org) within the OOD environment for remote visualization? In case you are not already familiar with it, VirtualGL allows the use of a headless GPU for 3D rendering using OpenGL. It is completely transparent to most OpenGL software, which just needs to be executed using the vglrun command. Currently, e.g., MATLAB runs on the cluster with software OpenGL emulation, making 3D visualization so slow as to be unusable. I primarily use the cluster for GPU computing anyway, so it would be great to be able to use the same GPU for visualization as well, rather than having to download computed results to my Mac to visualize them.
response:
I understand that you are interested in using VirtualGL for 3D rendering in your computational work on the FASRC cluster. However, as per the information from FASRC User Docs, no specific mention of VirtualGL installation is made and we do not have the permissions to install any software independently on these servers. As a result, it might not possible to directly use VirtualGL in the Open OnDemand environment on the FASRC cluster.
However, for doing 3D visualization or executing GPU-intensive jobs, you can use the GPU nodes available on the FASRC cluster. You can use an environment like MATLAB, which supports GPU calculations, for these purposes. MATLAB can be run using a GUI on a VDI (Virtual Desktop Infrastructure) session or on the command line while performing your computations on the GPU nodes, as the docs mention.
While this might not exactly replace the VirtualGL functionality, it might provide you with a workaround to meet your visualization needs within the limitations of the FASRC cluster.
Alternatively, you might reach out to FASRC support and request they look into the possibility of including VirtualGL in the future if it is congruent with their security and stability guidelines.
reference: Unfortunately GPU's have to either be in either compute mode or graphics mode. We can't put them in both. That said we have set aside one of our V100 nodes with Virtual GL in graphics mode for this exact purpose. You can find it in the remoteviz partition.

Description of problem:
I tried using conda/pip to install mpi4py using the openmpi installation in the system and it shows the following when I try to import mpi4py:

python: error: plugin_load_from_file: dlopen(/usr/lib64/slurm/auth_munge.so): /usr/lib64/slurm/auth_munge.so: undefined symbol: slurm_conf
python: error: Couldn't load specified plugin name for auth/munge: Dlopen of plugin file failed
python: error: cannot create auth context for auth/munge
python: fatal: failed to initialize auth plugin

Steps to Reproduce:
1. module load openmpi/4.1.5-fasrc03
2. export MPICC=$(which mpicc)
3. pip install mpi4py --no-cache-dir

Actual results:
python -c "from mpi4py import MPI"
python: error: plugin_load_from_file: dlopen(/usr/lib64/slurm/auth_munge.so): /usr/lib64/slurm/auth_munge.so: undefined symbol: slurm_conf
python: error: Couldn't load specified plugin name for auth/munge: Dlopen of plugin file failed
python: error: cannot create auth context for auth/munge
python: fatal: failed to initialize auth plugin


Expected results:
python -c "from mpi4py import MPI"
response:
It seems that the mpi4py module you're trying to import is not able to locate the correct shared library files. The plugin is looking for a Slurm auth plugin that it cannot find. The Slurm plugin may either not be installed, or it's installed in a location that's not on the library path.
For a quick fix, try setting the LD_LIBRARY_PATH environmental variable to the directory where the libmpi.so is, before running the Python command. You can find the location of libmpi.so by using the locate command.
However, generally, it's not recommended to use pip and conda directly on the FASRC cluster as it can lead to version conflicts and other issues. Instead, it is suggested to use Mamba, a faster and more efficient replacement for Conda with better dependency resolving features. You can install packages with Mamba within a specific environment which allows for better version control and isolation.
You can create a new environment using Mamba and install the desired packages in it. To do so:
bash
module load python/3.8.0-fasrc01
mamba create -n myenv
mamba activate myenv
mamba install mpi4py

This should install mpi4py in an environment that can be activated and deactivated as needed. The commands install mpi4py using the Mamba package manager, inside an environment named 'myenv'.
If this does not solve your issue, please let me know as there may be additional factors involved.

Verify your new password meets all requirements:

It should have both uppercase and lowercase letters.

It needs to include a number and a special character (!@#$%^&*).

It should not contain a portion of your name or username.

If you've done all of this and still can't reset your password:

You might be entering incorrect information too many times, and your account is locked. If your account gets locked, it should unlock by itself after about 5 to 10 minutes.

Otherwise, please make sure your computer’s time is in sync with FASRC servers’ time. The system might be prompting you for your password and verification code, or denying you access because your clock is off. Modern operating systems can be set to automatically maintain your correct timezone.

If none of the above works, I would recommend reaching out to the FASRC support team for further assistance.

As our lab's data continues to expand, we are facing the challenge of filling up our Tier 1 storage (Isilon, /n/spongebob_lab). To alleviate this issue and free up space, we are considering moving some older data from Tier 1 to Tier 3 tape storage.

However, I have encountered difficulty locating the endpoints of Tier 1 folders on Globus. This raises the question: is it not possible to directly transfer data from Tier 1 to Tier 3 using Globus, or am I simply unable to identify the correct path within Globus?

If indeed there are no endpoints for Tier 1 on Globus, I would greatly appreciate your guidance on the best practices for transferring data from Tier 1 to Tier 3. Would it be advisable to go through the scratch directory, following the route Isilon -> scratch -> Tier3?

In the event that direct transfer between Tier 1 and Tier 3 is not possible via Globus, the proposed route of Isilon -> scratch -> Tier 3 is an option to consider. Keep in mind that scratch storage has a 90-day retention policy.
However, I would highly recommend contacting the FASRC support team for their suggestions as well. They can provide the most accurate information and may have alternative options that are more effective for your use case.

user_input: I am writing to inquire if there is an easy way to upload sequence files to NCBI. NCBI provides an FTP site for us to upload files. However, I noticed that FASRC supports SFTP but not FTP. Is there a way to conveniently upload files through FTP?
response:
FASRC does not directly support FTP file transfers, only SFTP and SCP due to their secure nature. While FTP is traditionally used for web servers, SFTP and SCP are more commonly used when dealing with larger data transfers on computing resources.
That being said, for uploading sequence files to NCBI, you can utilize the SFTP connection through a client like Filezilla (as outlined in the FASRC User Docs) or through SCP commands in the terminal. Here are the general steps:
Download and install Filezilla or any other SFTP client.

Setup a new connection in your SFTP client with the NCBI provided details.

Browse to the files that you want to upload on your local machine within the SFTP client,

Drag and drop (or use the upload command) to transfer files to the NCBI FTP server.

Remember to replace the ftp:// with sftp:// in the NCBI provided FTP host, as you are making an SFTP connection.
If you're more comfortable using the terminal, you can utilize SCP. Here's an example:
scp /path/to/local/file username@ftp.ncbi.nih.gov:/path/to/remote/directory
Replace "username" with your specific NCBI username, and adjust the paths as needed. You'll be prompted to enter your password.
For both methods, remember to stay within your allocated data storage limit on the NCBI server.
Doing this implies that NCBI has SFTP available, and you have the needed access. If FTP must be used, you would need to transfer the files to a local machine and upload them through FTP from there, as FTP is insecure and therefore not directly supported on FASRC.

user_input: I can connect to the FASSE VPN (it says Connected to vpn.rc.fas.harvard.edu), but I cannot access the FASSE dashboard website. I have tried resetting my computer, reinstalling the Cisc VPN, and different browsers. I always get the following error.
response:
From the error message, it appears the problem might be related to connectivity issues. However, please finance that you were connected to the right VPN realm.
When logging into the FASSE VPN, you need to use your username appended with "@fasse" (Example: username@fasse). This ensures you're in the correct VPN realm to access the FASSE dashboard.
If you're using the correct VPN realm and the problem persists, it might be a proxy issue. In the FASSE environment, accessing the internet must be done through a network proxy. You can manually set the proxy in your terminal environment with the following commands:
export http_proxy=http://rcproxy.rc.fas.harvard.edu:3128
export https_proxy=http://rcproxy.rc.fas.harvard.edu:3128
If these steps don't solve your problem, I recommend reaching out to FASRC support for additional assistance.

user_input: I ran out of memory. How do I increase it?
response:
To increase the memory for your job in Slurm, you will need to set a larger limit by modifying your batch script or job submission command. In Slurm, you set memory limits using the #SBATCH --mem X parameter in your job script, where X is the maximum amount of memory your job will use per node, in megabytes (MB).
Use the following steps to increase your memory limit:
Determine an appropriate value for memory consumption. If you're unsure, start relatively large. For instance, job slots on average have about 4000 MB per core.

Modify your job submission script or command to include a larger --mem value.
For example,

bash

#SBATCH --mem 8000
This sets the memory limit to be 8000 MB or 8 GB for that job.

Submit the job again.

Remember, setting the memory limit too high will make it harder for the scheduler to find space to run your job. On the other hand, setting it too low increases the likelihood of your job running out of memory.
You can monitor your jobs' memory usage with the seff JOBID command, where JOBID is the ID of the job you're interested in. This will give you information on memory usage for that job. Use this information to tweak your memory request as needed to optimize resource usage. You should set your memory request to something a little larger than what seff reports, since you're defining a hard upper limit.
If your job is repeatedly running out of memory, review your code for potential optimizations, or consider whether the task can be split into smaller, less memory-intensive parts.

user_input: What’s the difference of memory and gpu memory?
response:
Memory often refers to the Random Access Memory (RAM), which is used to store data that the computer's processor needs quick access to. It's the memory available for the CPU and all its non-GPU processes, including the data you load into a program, objects your code creates, and the code itself.
GPU memory, on the other hand, refers to the memory that is exclusively used by a graphics processing unit (GPU) when performing tasks such as rendering graphics or numerical computation, often for machine learning tasks. GPU memory is used to store data that the GPU needs immediate access to when executing GPU related tasks, like texture data, vertices, or the machine learning model parameters.
Therefore, when a job is submitted, it must specify how much CPU memory and GPU memory it needs in order to perform its tasks without running out of space. Generally, these memory allocations will be used distinctly depending upon the nature of the computational task. If the computations are primarily being done on the GPU, then it would need more GPU memory, while if the computations are being done on the CPU, it would need more CPU memory.
